newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Belgian deputy PM's fate hangs in the balance.
newsitem.headline: Belgian deputy PM's fate hangs in the balance.

text.p: Belgian Deputy Prime Minister Elio Di Rupo's fate hung in the balance early on Thursday as a parliamentary commission, examining allegations Di Rupo had sex with minors, failed to reach a rapid conclusion.

The minister, who hotly denies the allegations, was heard by the 11-member panel of fellow politicians for some two hours on Wednesday evening, but the commission was still in session at 2330 GMT, some nine hours after deliberations began.
Di Rupo, 45 and a discreet homesexual, insists that he only ever has sex with consenting adults. Homosexuality is not a crime in Belgium, but sex with children younger than 16 is.

The commission has to judge whether the evidence as presented in a confidential report by the Brussels public prosecutor is strong enough to send Di Rupo before the Cour de Cassation, the country's highest court.

A political source said in parliament in the early hours of Thursday that opinions within the commission were still far apart. He added the prosecutor's dossier was not strong enough to send Di Rupo before the court without reasonable doubt.

A referral to the Cour, the only court that can try ministers and ex-ministers, would certainly end the career of the second highest cabinet official. A simple majority in parliament is needed to implement the panel's recommendation.
Some analysts doubted Di Rupo could survive politically, even if the commision of peers felt there was no case to answer.
Parliamentarians of the VLD opposition have said the allegations are enough in themselves to do fatal damage to Di Rupo's ability to function as a minister.
His defence before the commission, laying bare intimate aspects of his sexual life, can only have made it harder for Di Rupo to be seen as just another minister by his peers.

The allegations, following an unrelated paedophile sex and murder scandal that has shaken Belgium for the past three months, have further eroded public confidence in the political and judicial system and shaken the government.

A telephone poll of 1,000 people by La Derniere Heure newspaper showed 49 percent thought Di Rupo should quit immediately against 42 percent who believed it was not necessary. Di Rupo has made it clear he will fight to the end.
Some commission members also said the case was thin.

"We are looking into the possibility of letting Mr Di Rupo be heard by the court without going through the heavy procedure (of lifting his constitutional immunity)," commission member Albert Gehlen earlier told reporters in parliament.
BRTN radio said the Brussels public prosecutor had asked the commission to take this course.
Gehlen belongs to the francophone Christian Democrats -- one of four parties in Belgium's centre-left ruling coalition.
Parliament has three options when it comes to a vote.
It can adopt the prosecutor's request and bring Di Rupo before the court. It can reject the request, or it can allow the court to continue the investigation against Di Rupo.
In the last case suspicion against Di Rupo would persist and his position as minister would be shaky to say the least.
A date for a parliamentary vote on the commission's recommendation has not yet been set.
Some analysts have said, however, that a continued investigation would be in the interest of the ruling coalition.
A resignation would create a political vacuum since there is a shortage of successors among the francophone Socialists.
Two years ago three leading members of Di Rupo's party lost their jobs in a bribery affair which also forced Willy Claes to resign as Nato secretary-general in October 1995.
A collapse of the party over a succession battle could mean the end of the ruling coalition.
